analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a court order before running facial recognition searches and bans real-time face surveillance.
analysis.headline: The Facial Recognition Act of 2023 was never taken up by either committee it was referred to, and died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set the first federal rules for how police use facial recognition. Officers would need a court order, based on probable cause of a serious crime, before searching databases of driver's license photos, passport photos, or arrest photos. It bans using the technology for real-time tracking and surveillance, on body and dashboard cameras, or to enforce immigration law; it requires annual accuracy and bias testing, public reporting and audits, notice to people identified by the technology, and lets people sue for $50,000 per violation when police use it unlawfully. States that don't comply would lose 15% of a federal justice grant.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose photo sits in a government database — effectively everyone with a driver's license, passport, or prior arrest. The people most directly protected are those wrongly identified by inaccurate systems, people arrested but never charged (whose photos must be purged from databases used for searches), and people of color, on whom misidentification errors fall hardest.

how_it_helps.text: Police could only search reference photo databases (driver's licenses, passports, arrest photos) with a court order requiring probable cause of a serious felony-level offense, with narrow emergencies like AMBER Alerts and immediate danger of death allowed first and a 12-hour deadline to get a judge's approval afterward.

The bill bans facial recognition used for real-time face surveillance, on body cameras, dashboard cameras, aircraft, and drones, and bans its use to track people exercising First Amendment rights or to enforce immigration law.

Every system would need annual National Institute of Standards and Technology benchmark testing and independent operational testing for accuracy and for error rates that vary by race, ethnicity, gender, or age, and systems that fail could not be used.

A facial recognition match could not be the sole basis for an arrest or search warrant, judges would get public annual reports on orders issued, and the Government Accountability Office would audit federal agencies — with agencies suspended from using the technology until violations are fixed.

People identified or misidentified in violation of the bill could sue for damages of $50,000 per violation or the government's profits, plus attorney's fees, and the bill strips state immunity from such suits.
Arrest photo databases would have to purge photos of minors, people released without charge, and people acquitted, every six months.

analysis.who_pays: Facial recognition vendors selling to police, and law enforcement agencies, which would lose the ability to run unchecked searches; a small cost falls on taxpayers through $5 million a year for NIST testing and compliance staff time at police departments and courts.

drawbacks.text: The warrant requirement and documentation duties could add time and cost to investigations in which identifying a suspect through other means has already failed — precisely the cases the bill targets.

The bill leaves broad carve-outs: police may still use facial recognition without any court order on people during booking and custody, and the emergency exception lets officers search first and seek approval up to 12 hours later.

Enforcement leans on lawsuits with a $50,000 per-violation damages figure and a good-faith reliance defense for officers acting on a court order or honest reading of the law, which critics could argue either over-penalizes agencies or under-deters misconduct depending on their view.

It regulates only law enforcement use; commercial and private-sector facial recognition, including scraping of public photos by firms like Clearview AI for sales to police, is largely untouched outside the rules on what databases officers may search.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: police and vendors give up cheap, unreviewed access to photo databases of millions of people, and in exchange the public gets a warrant requirement, bias testing, and a way to sue when the technology is misused. The genuine weaknesses are the booking and emergency carve-outs and the narrow scope covering only law enforcement, not commercial surveillance. On balance the bill is a serious, detailed attempt to fix a documented problem — wrongful arrests from faulty matches — without banning the technology outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2023 and referred to the Judiciary and Science, Space, and Technology Committees, neither of which ever held a hearing or markup, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on October 26, 2023, with five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Jackson Lee, Clarke, Gomez, Ivey, and Veasey.
The same day it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.
That referral was the last action of any kind recorded for the bill; no hearing, markup, vote, or further consideration ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors are better off: they continue running searches against driver's license and arrest photo databases with no federal warrant requirement, no bias testing mandate, and no civil liability. The public gets none of the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and surveillance tech vendors

for.name: Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Facial Recognition Act of 2023 and shepherded its referral to two committees.

for.name: Sheila Jackson Lee, Yvette Clarke, Jimmy Gomez, Glenn Ivey, and Marc Veasey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's five original cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — over the remaining fourteen months of the Congress.

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Also never acted on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the House majority never scheduled any action on the bill.

industries.note: Companies selling search tools against driver's license, passport, and arrest databases — including firms like Clearview AI that scrape public photos — would face warrant-based demand, mandatory accuracy and bias testing, bans on surveillance uses, and clients suspended for violations. Their business model of unreviewed bulk searches against government photo troves is what the bill targets.

Police and prosecutors would lose unilateral access to photo databases, face logging, reporting, GAO and state audits, and civil suits of $50,000 per violation. Their interest in unrestricted searches runs against the public's interest in not being misidentified or tracked.

DMVs would have to post public notices about facial recognition searches of license photos, restrict bulk photo transfers to law enforcement, and operate searches only under court orders — a compliance burden, but one that closes a little-known backdoor into license databases.
